text: Berrien Springs is a village in Berrien County, Michigan, with a population of 1,910 as recorded in the 2020 census. It is located within Oronoko Charter Township and is named after John M. Berrien, with "Springs" added due to the discovery of mineral springs in the area. The village marks the earliest European-American settlement in Oronoko Township, originally known as "Wolf's Prairie," named after a Potawatomi chief named Wolf who led a village on a 1,000-acre prairie. The first permanent European-American settlers, John Pike and his family, arrived in 1829. Francis B. Murdoch, a co-founder of the village and the first lawyer in Berrien County (spelled 'Murdock' in some records), built a two-story log house in 1831, which is the oldest surviving example of its kind in Michigan. This house was moved in 1973 to near courthouse square as part of a historic complex. Murdoch was active during the Antebellum period in representing enslaved African Americans in freedom suits, under Michigan’s principle of "once free, always free," which granted freedom to enslaved individuals brought into the state. The village was platted in 1831, and its post office opened as "Berrien" on December 4, 1832, later changing to "Berrien Springs" on April 18, 1836. Berrien Springs served as the county seat from 1837 until 1894, when St. Joseph became the county seat. The Berrien Springs courthouse, designed by local architect Gilbert B. Avery and completed in 1839, is the oldest courthouse in Michigan and features Greek Revival architecture with large columns, a triangular pediment, and white paint. After the county seat moved in 1894, the building was used for various purposes and briefly vacant, with restoration efforts beginning in 1967 and completed by 1975. The restored courthouse square includes the Midwest’s most complete surviving mid-nineteenth century county government complex and currently houses a county museum and archives, serving as headquarters for the Berrien County Historical Association, with its original buildings listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The village was once known as the Christmas pickle capital of the world, with a Pickle Festival established by the Berrien Springs-Eau Claire Chamber of Commerce, the Berrien County Historical Association, and the village, featuring parades, games, and a Pickle Prince and Princess contest that ran until the mid-2000s. The festival was revived in 2021 by the Village, the BCHA, and the Berrien Springs Community Library. The village has a total area of 1.02 square miles (2.64 km²), of which 0.94 square miles (2.43 km²) is land and 0.08 square miles (0.21 km²) is water, situated on the St. Joseph River. As of the 2010 census, there were 1,800 people, 756 households, and 463 families, with a population density of 1,914.9 per square mile (739.3/km²) and 837 housing units at an average density of 890.4 per square mile (343.8/km²). The racial makeup was 72.7% White, 12.9% African American, 0.4% Native American, 5.1% Asian, 0.4% Pacific Islander, 3.8% from other races, and 4.7% from two or more races, with 12.9% of the population identifying as Hispanic or Latino. Household data showed 30.2% had children under 18, 40.9% were married couples, 16.0% had a female householder with no husband, 4.4% had a male householder with no wife, and 38.8% were non-families; 32.0% were made up of individuals, and 11.2% had someone 65 or older living alone. The average household size was 2.35 and average family size was 2.95. The median age was 34.6 years, with 22.8% under 18, 13.1% aged 18–24, 27.2% aged 25–44, 23.3% aged 45–64, and 13.7% aged 65 or older; the gender makeup was 47.9% male and 52.1% female. In 2000, the population was 1,862, with 732 households and 475 families, a population density of 2,059.6 per square mile (795.2/km²), and 787 housing units at an average density of 870.5 per square mile (336.1/km²). Racial makeup was 77.12% White, 11.06% African American, 0.43% Native American, 4.03% Asian, 0.16% Pacific Islander, 4.30% from other races, and 2.90% from two or more races, with 8.92% identifying as Hispanic or Latino. Household data showed 30.2% had children under 18, 49.2% were married couples, 11.6% had a female householder with no husband, and 35.0% were non-families; 29.8% were made up of individuals, and 10.7% had someone 65 or older living alone. The average household size was 2.46 and average family size was 3.05. The median age was 36 years, with 23.0% under 18, 11.9% aged 18–24, 28.7% aged 25–44, 21.0% aged 45–64, and 15.3% aged 65 or older; for every 100 females, there were 95.0 males, and for every 100 females aged 18 and over, there were 88.1 males. The median household income was $32,396, median family income was $41,250, males had a median income of $31,467, and females had $21,750; per capita income was $16,093. About 12.4% of families and 17.5% of the population were below the poverty line, including 25.4% of those under 18 and 4.1% of those aged 65 or older.
